---
title: "Empirical Distributions: Let the Record Speak"
---

A potential profile can describe a proposed source. We can also build one from the observations themselves.

Each occurrence contributes one unit of weight to its observed value.

## 🔰 Count the record {#sec-sample-empirical-distributions-count-the-record}

For a record with $n>0$ observations, define

$$
c_S[f]=\sum_{t=1}^{n}\mathbf1_{\{S[t]=f\}}.
$$

The indicator contributes one whenever the observation matches $f$.

The presentation's 28 die throws are

$$
\begin{gathered}
1,6,2,5,4,6,3,2,4,1,3,5,2,6,\\
4,1,3,5,4,6,2,3,1,4,5,6,2,3.
\end{gathered}
$$

Their face counts are

$$
(c_S[1],\ldots,c_S[6])=(4,5,5,5,4,5).
$$

Every observation contributes once, so the counts total exactly 28.

## 🏵 Normalize the counts {#sec-sample-empirical-distributions-normalize-the-counts}

The empirical probability mass function is

$$
\widehat p_S[f]=\frac{c_S[f]}n.
$$

This is an exact description of the unweighted record. The denominator equals the observation count, not approximately but exactly.

It is also the probability law obtained by choosing one of the observed addresses uniformly at random and returning its value.

That interpretation gives the empirical distribution a concrete generator: resample the recorded observations with replacement.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sample-empirical-profile
#| fig-cap: "The original 28 observations and their empirical probability profile. The horizontal reference is the proposed fair-die law, not an assumed property of the unknown source."
#| fig-alt: "A sequence of 28 die outcomes is shown above a six-bar empirical distribution with counts four, five, five, five, four, five and a reference line at one sixth."
#| fig-format: svg
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rolls = np.array([
    1, 6, 2, 5, 4, 6, 3, 2, 4, 1, 3, 5, 2, 6,
    4, 1, 3, 5, 4, 6, 2, 3, 1, 4, 5, 6, 2, 3
])
faces = np.arange(1, 7)
counts = np.bincount(rolls, minlength=7)[1:7]
figure, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9, 5.5), layout="constrained")
axes[0].plot(np.arange(1, rolls.size + 1), rolls, "o-", color="#236B8E", linewidth=0.8)
axes[0].set(xlabel="Observation address", ylabel="Face", yticks=faces)
axes[1].bar(faces, counts / rolls.size, color="#236B8E")
axes[1].axhline(1 / 6, color="#A54B30", linestyle="--", label="Fair-die reference")
axes[1].set(xlabel="Face", ylabel="Empirical probability", xticks=faces, ylim=(0, 0.23))
axes[1].legend(frameon=False)
for axis in axes:
    axis.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.15)
    axis.set_axisbelow(True)
plt.show()
```

## ⚙️ The mean can be read from either representation {#sec-sample-empirical-distributions-the-mean-can-be-read-from-either-representation}

Grouping observations by their values gives

$$
\frac1n\sum_tS[t]
=
\sum_f f\,\widehat p_S[f].
$$

The sample mean is exactly the expected value under the empirical distribution.

For the 28 throws, it is $99/28\approx3.536$. The proposed fair-die generator has mean $3.5$. Those are different objects: a summary of this record and a property of a model.

The equality in the display does not equate the observed mean with the mean of the unknown source.

## 💡 A histogram changes what remains visible {#sec-sample-empirical-distributions-a-histogram-changes-what-remains-visible}

Counts discard the original observation order. They can be sufficient for some questions about independent repeated draws while missing the transitions needed to study a source with memory.

Real-valued measurements also have a discrete empirical distribution: each recorded value carries its observed share of the mass. Drawing a histogram density adds bins. For a bin of width $w$, its density height is

$$
\frac{\text{observations in bin}}{nw}.
$$

Multiplying the height by the width recovers the bin's relative frequency.

## ☯ Description becomes estimation through assumptions {#sec-sample-empirical-distributions-description-becomes-estimation-through-assumptions}

Under independent, identically distributed sampling, the relative frequency of each fixed event converges to its probability as the record grows. Other sampling structures need their own arguments.

A source that tosses a coin once and repeats forever has an empirical profile concentrated on one outcome in every run. The record does not approach a half-and-half profile.

Also, signed differences between two normalized probability profiles always sum to zero. That cancellation cannot establish that the profiles agree.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try the idea {#sec-sample-empirical-distributions-try-the-idea}

A record contains $2,2,5$. Write its empirical law and mean. Can we conclude that a value absent from the record is impossible for the original generator?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Work it through {#sec-sample-empirical-distributions-work-it-through}

The empirical law gives mass $2/3$ to two and $1/3$ to five, with mean three. It assigns zero to unseen values as a description of this record. Their true generating probabilities may still be positive.
:::
